utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as the court knows, Judge Robinson and I are sitting alone today and, indeed, for the rest of this week, probably, since Judge Bennouna is sitting in the Appeal Chamber on a hearing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We understand that as to -- is it the first three days, that's covered by the Rule, and as the last two days, by agreement of the parties. But something to that effect, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it partly depends how long the hearing in the Appeal Chamber goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I raise a few administrative matters before the witness is called. First, last week's last witness, Zoran Maric, was a witness in respect of whom there was considerable pressure to have him finished last week, and we managed to achieve that by the end of Friday afternoon. It was only on the basis that a large part of what I would have asked him about necessarily was abandoned. I'm quite happy about that, but I think probably I ought, where it was so substantial, the amount that was abandoned, to record at least for the record some of the topics I simply wasn't in a position to cover in the time available. And I didn't cover the second half of '92, I didn't deal with the considerable quantity of documents he produced, I wasn't able to cover the numerous affidavits in support, or deal with his account of the start of the war, or what he said about Mr. Hadzimelic. If I turn to this week, we received yesterday, in the afternoon, a couple of summaries, one for the first witness and one, I think, for the second or third. These witnesses are political, and although I'm not objecting to them on the grounds that they are experts, they are very close to being expert in some of their content, and therefore I need considerably more assistance than I do for ordinary fact witnesses. Thus the presence here today -- the Chamber knows what I said last week about accommodation, and if the Chamber has any ability to influence accommodation available to this Chamber, I would be grateful for any help it can give, for, as you'll see, the problem relates not just to this week's witnesses but, I suspect, to the witnesses who are to follow. The current interpretation on the requirement to provide a witness list, so far as the Defence is concerned, is to give only a fortnight, and that means, as I understand it, where there's a week where we're not sitting, like next week, we know nothing more than the witnesses for this week. That is to be contrasted with what the Prosecution provided, which was never less than six weeks and as long as possible, right up to the end of the case. We were served with two expert reports last Monday and three more yesterday. Now, that means that the earliest date upon which experts could be called as to the two would be the week of the 20th, and as to the three, would be the week of the 26th. Calling those witnesses on those weeks would, of course, give us the minimum time to prepare for them, and of course it can't be that those are already planned dates, because no doubt the Defence would have told us about them if they were. However, if it's any -- if there is an intention to call those expert witnesses as soon as that, and I again remind the Chamber that we spread our experts throughout the evidence and gave as much notice as we possibly could, but if there's any intention to call experts on the weeks of the 20th or the 26th, I may be in difficulties if I cannot obtain the necessary assistance in relation to those expert reports in the time available. I'm not here simply to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if we can deal with this. What are you asking?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm simply serving notice of two things, really. One, of course I'll do everything I can to ensure I'm properly equipped with expert opinion to cross-examine these witnesses, but I'm not going to cross-examine witnesses without the appropriate expertise, so that it will help if the Defence will tell us when these witnesses are scheduled. I will try and make arrangements accordingly, and those arrangements will, of course, include having, it may be, those witnesses available in court to assist me while the Defence witnesses are giving evidence, particularly where those experts are themselves attacked in strong terms in the Defence expert's report. But generally, and again the Chamber will recall, that my suggestion right at beginning was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... conventionally regarded, in some places, as the most helpful. But I must serve notice that it is by no means guaranteed that I will be able, in all cases, to be properly equipped to cross-examine these experts if they are called in the weeks of the 20th or the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question which we have to ask first is that you require these experts to give evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, in all cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- or to be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in respect of at least one, there may be preliminary arguments about admissibility. So that's a problem, and I think the answer is for the Defence to give us as much notice as they can as to their witness list and to ask to see what problems there may be. Experts will, of course, once again create problems of accommodation. Those are the only matters that are general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with this one first. Mr. Sayers, when is it proposed to call these experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two experts will be called during the week of the 20th as our third and fourth witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be subject to our agreement, before you make that arrangement. Which two are those?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Schrader will be the fourth witness, and Professor Jankovich, the Zenica shelling expert, will be the third witness that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are their topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Dr. Schrader is a military expert who will provide a variety of insights as to troop dispositions, strategic plans and so forth along the lines of Mr. Elford, but his report is somewhat more detailed. And Professor Jankovich is an artillery ballistics expert who will provide testimony, as I forecast earlier in a very abbreviated fashion, related to the Zenica shelling allegations made by the Prosecution in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other experts?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There are two -- there are three other experts, Your Honour; Dr. Stjepan Mestrovic, who is a sociologist, and we propose to call him during the week of the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What relevant evidence does he give?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He addresses the evidence offered by Dr. Allcock and others. Then there is a historian by the name of Mark Almond from the Oriel College, Oxford, who addresses historical issues of the type reviewed by Dr. Donia in the Prosecution case. And then our final expert, who we haven't actually lined up to testify yet at any specific point, is Bruce Koenig, who is the audiotape expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Almond is the week of the 26th?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other one is undecided and undated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Correct. He will not testify during the week of the 26th, I can assure the Court of that, or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And so far you've served Dr. Schrader and Professor Jankovich; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've served all of them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They haven't come through to us. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And if I could just explain to the Court, in conformity with the plan that we've had throughout the Defence case, we're trying to present discreet areas of testimony with all of the witnesses relating to a particular area, such as, for the last two weeks, the Busovaca witnesses testified. This week we propose to have people who occupy prominent positions on the national level testify, two confidential witnesses, two in open session, and then next week there will be two more witnesses along those lines, the former Minister of Justice, Mr. Buntic, and a minister of reconstruction in the HR HB government, Mr. Robovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will stay within relevant lines on these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. We have borne that in mind, and I hope the Trial Chamber will appreciate that working with these witnesses to keep outlines within the relevant lines presents some challenges, and I hope and I think we have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, now that we know the time table, we will make arrangements we can and I will report back as soon as I have results, but with short notice I may not be able to secure the assistance I wish. Can I turn please lastly to today's witness -- are we now in closed session or private session? Can I make the observation in open session then? If necessary, we can go to private session for the usual reasons. We know nothing of the grounds upon which closed session is sought because these matters were dealt with ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we would challenge the appropriateness of this witness giving evidence in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we bear that in mind, we'll call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the witness comes in, on behalf of the two accused, Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez, to seek apologies for being without their jackets today. Something happened with the transport and they lost their jackets on the way. That's what I rose to say. I apologise on their behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to apologise for that. If they feel more comfortable without their jackets, they can come without their jackets it's a matter for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have said one other thing while the witness is coming in, for reasons that I shan't go into at the moment, I definitely will not be able to conclude my cross-examination of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's listed for two days anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 4.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of June, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
